denomFacts.question: Which movements are growing fastest?
denomFacts.claim: Pentecostal, charismatic and independent churches in the Global South are the fastest-growing part of Christianity.
denomFacts.answer: Yes, with caveats about definitions. Pentecostals and charismatics grew from under a million in 1900 to about 664 million in 2025, and Independents from about 9 million to about 409 million (CSGC). Growth is concentrated in Africa and Asia, while Catholics grew by about 0.6 per cent a year in 2020–25.
denomFacts.explanation:
The Center for the Study of Global Christianity's long-term series shows the most dramatic change of the last century: the rise of 'renewalists'—Pentecostals, charismatics in older churches, and independent neo-charismatics. Their share of all Christians has risen from almost nothing in 1900 to about a quarter today.

The Independent megabloc, which includes African Initiated Churches, Chinese house churches and independent Pentecostal networks, has grown more than forty-fold since 1900. Evangelicals, defined as members of evangelical churches, numbered about 420 million in 2025. By contrast, the Catholic and Orthodox populations are growing more slowly than the world population as a whole.

Regional growth matters as much as denominational. Africa had about 754 million Christians in 2025 and is growing fastest, through both high birth rates and conversion; Asia has about 417 million, and growth in China, India and Iran is significant though hard to measure. In Europe and North America many historic churches are shrinking.

The figures have limitations: 'Pentecostal/charismatic' overlaps with every other megabloc, and surveys in some countries (notably China) cannot be verified. Pew's projections also stress demography: much of Christianity's future growth is driven by birth rates in sub-Saharan Africa rather than conversions.

denomFacts.question: Where do most Christians live now?
denomFacts.claim: Most Christians now live in the Global South—Africa, Latin America and Asia.
denomFacts.answer: Yes. According to the Center for the Study of Global Christianity, 69 per cent of Christians lived in the Global South in 2025, compared with less than a fifth in 1900, and the share is projected to reach 78 per cent by 2050. Africa now has more Christians than any other continent.
denomFacts.explanation:
In 1900 about four in five Christians lived in Europe and North America. During the twentieth century, missionary expansion, conversion and population growth in Africa, Latin America and Asia shifted the centre of gravity of world Christianity southwards, a change described by Andrew Walls, Lamin Sanneh and Philip Jenkins.

The CSGC estimated about 754 million Christians in Africa and about 620 million in Latin America in 2025, with about 417 million in Asia. The Catholic Church's own statistics for 2024 show that 20.3 per cent of Catholics now live in Africa, slightly more than in Europe (20.2 per cent), while the Americas hold 47.7 per cent.

The largest Christian populations by country include the United States, Brazil, Mexico, the Philippines, Russia, Nigeria, China and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Pew Research Center's 2025 report found that in 2020 sub-Saharan Africa had overtaken Europe as the region with the most Christians.

The shift changes what 'typical' Christianity looks like: younger, poorer, more often Pentecostal or charismatic, more conservative on moral questions, and often living as a minority alongside Muslims, Hindus or Buddhists.

denomFacts.question: Why do churches divide?
denomFacts.claim: Christian divisions are simply about doctrine.
denomFacts.answer: Doctrine matters, but most major divisions mixed theology with questions of authority, politics, language, culture, ethnicity, worship and personality. Many splits that look doctrinal were also about who governs the church and whose culture it reflects.
denomFacts.explanation:
Some divisions are primarily doctrinal: the Arian controversy over the deity of Christ, the Christological disputes after Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451), and the Reformation's arguments over justification and the Eucharist. Yet even these were entangled with other factors: the post-Chalcedonian split followed linguistic and regional lines (Greek against Coptic, Syriac and Armenian) and resentment of Byzantine imperial power.

Authority is a recurring cause. The East–West schism of 1054 turned as much on papal claims as on the Filioque; Vatican I's definition of papal infallibility (1870) produced the Old Catholics; Protestant disputes repeatedly concern who interprets Scripture. Politics and empire shaped the English Reformation (Henry VIII's marriage, 1534), Orthodox autocephaly disputes such as Ukraine's (2018–19), and the Church of the East's separation in Persia.

Worship and practice have split churches too: the Russian Old Believers (1666) over the sign of the cross and liturgical books, the Churches of Christ over organs, and Orthodox Old Calendarists over the calendar (1924). Ethnicity and race drove the formation of the African Methodist Episcopal Church (1816), the Southern Baptist Convention's split over slavery (1845), the Bulgarian Exarchate (1872) and many African Initiated Churches that rejected missionary control.

Moral questions, especially slavery in the nineteenth century and sexuality today, have divided Methodists, Anglicans, Lutherans and Presbyterians. Personalities matter, as in the Brethren schism of 1848 between J. N. Darby and B. W. Newton's supporters, and mission fields exported the divisions of sending churches. Conversely, many unions—the Church of South India (1947), the Lutheran–Catholic Joint Declaration (1999)—show that divisions can be overcome when the non-doctrinal causes fade.

denomFacts.question: How many Christians are there in India and which churches?
denomFacts.claim: Christians are 2.3 per cent of India's population.
denomFacts.answer: That is the official figure: the 2011 Census counted 27.8 million Christians, 2.3 per cent of the population. Other estimates are higher (Pew put it at about 31.8 million in 2010, and some Christian researchers higher still), partly because Dalit converts may record themselves as Hindu to keep Scheduled Caste benefits.
denomFacts.explanation:
The Census of India 2011 counted 27,819,588 Christians. They are unevenly spread: Christians are the majority in Nagaland (88 per cent), Mizoram (87 per cent) and Meghalaya (75 per cent), and form large minorities in Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa (25 per cent) and Kerala, where 6.14 million Christians made up 18.4 per cent of the state. Tamil Nadu had 4.42 million (6.1 per cent), and there are large communities among the Adivasi peoples of Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.

Official numbers may undercount. Under the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order of 1950, Scheduled Caste status—and with it reservations in education and employment—is limited to Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists, so some Dalit Christians are recorded as Hindu. Independent researchers, including the Pew Forum (2011) and the World Christian Database, therefore give higher estimates. The next census, delayed from 2021, is scheduled for 2026–27.

The Catholic Church is the largest single church, with three rites: the Latin Church, the Syro-Malabar Church (the largest Eastern Catholic church after the Ukrainian, based in Kerala) and the Syro-Malankara Church. The Orthodox Thomas Christian churches—the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church and the Jacobite Syrian Church—and the reformed Mar Thoma Church are concentrated in Kerala.

Among Protestants, the united Church of South India (1947) and Church of North India (1970) are the largest mainline bodies; Baptist conventions dominate Nagaland and much of the North-east, and the Presbyterian Church of India (Welsh Calvinistic Methodist in origin) dominates Mizoram and Meghalaya. Lutheran churches (the Tamil Evangelical Lutheran Church, the Andhra Evangelical Lutheran Church and the Gossner church in Jharkhand), Methodists and the Salvation Army are also significant, and Pentecostal churches such as the Indian Pentecostal Church of God, together with many independent congregations, are the fastest-growing part of Indian Christianity.
